:question/worked-solution "First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=40
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-8.$ 

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)1I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-8)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard $$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=40
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-8.$ 

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)1I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-8)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/worked-solution "First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=48
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$"] [17592186162668 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] :tutorial/content "Let $A$ be a $2\\times 2$ symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables \n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}=P\\mathbf{y}\n$$\n\nthat transforms the quadratic form $\\mathbf{x}^TA\\mathbf{x}$ into the quadratic form $\\mathbf{y}^TD\\mathbf{y},$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. \n\nThe columns of the matrix $P$ are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of $A,$ which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the **principal axes** of the quadratic form.\n\nLet's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation \n\n$$\n6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,\n$$\n\nand see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.\n\nIf we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:\n\n![](images/d8/d8a6b6dff52e0c4004432f9447b5fd484612eaacf07588c3469af143b0a9e880.png)\n\nIt looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.\n\nFirst, we consider the corresponding quadratic form \n\n$$\nQ(\\mathbf{x})={\\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\\color{blue}3}x_2^2,\n$$\n\nwhich we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form. \n\nSo, we write down the matrix of $Q(\\mathbf{x}) \\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 3\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nNext, we find the eigenvalues of $A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}|A-\\lambda I| & =0 \\\\ |\\begin{aligned}6-\\lambda  & 2 \\\\ 2 & 3-\\lambda \\end{aligned}| & =0 \\\\ {\\lambda }^{2}-9\\lambda +14 & =0 \\\\ \\lambda  & =7,\\,2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's find the principal axes of the curve.\n\n- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)\\mathbf{x}=\\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]$ Dividing $\\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\\| \\mathbf{v}_1  \\| = \\sqrt{5},$ we get \n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\n- Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\\mathbf{x}=\\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}]$ Dividing $\\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\\| \\mathbf{v}_2  \\| = \\sqrt{5},$ we get \n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nTherefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are\n\n$\\qquad$ $[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]$ and $[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}]$\n\nNotice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes $y_1$ and $y_2.$ \n\n![](images/10/10a2f0ccd179eba7f65410f932548d954a459e1bc8dcb0803a5b2d9fe7896432.png)\n\nIn the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to \n\n$$\n7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.\n$$\n\n \n\nTherefore, the curve has the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2} & =14 \\\\ \\frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis is an ellipse with semiaxes $\\sqrt2$ and $\\sqrt{7}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid
